title: Indian manuscripts: birch bark, palm leaf and paper
seo_title: Indian Manuscripts: Birch Bark, Palm Leaf, Paper and NMM
meta_description: Indian manuscripts explained: birch bark, palm leaf and paper, how they were made and copied, the oldest survivors, and the National Mission for Manuscripts.
keywords: how palm leaf manuscripts were made
summary: Indian manuscripts are hand-written texts on birch bark, palm leaf and, from around the 13th to 14th centuries in many regions, paper. Millions survive in libraries, temples, monasteries and homes, in dozens of scripts and languages. The National Mission for Manuscripts, set up in 2003, works to document, conserve and digitise them.

sections.h2: Why India has so many manuscripts
paras: India's learned traditions relied on copying. Texts on grammar, philosophy, medicine, astronomy, law, poetry and ritual were copied again and again by scribes, students and scholars, because the materials decayed in a humid climate within a few centuries. Each surviving manuscript is usually a copy of a copy, and many of the oldest texts are known only from manuscripts written more than a thousand years after the text was composed.

The result is one of the largest manuscript heritages in the world. Estimates run into the millions, held by public libraries, universities, temples, maths, Jain bhandaras, Buddhist monasteries, mosques and madrasas, and private families. They are written in Sanskrit, Prakrit, Pali, Tamil, Persian, Arabic, Tibetan and most regional languages, in dozens of scripts. The [ancient scripts of India](ancient-scripts-of-india.html) guide explains where those scripts came from.

In the north-west and Kashmir, the inner bark of the Himalayan birch (Betula utilis) was peeled into thin sheets, smoothed, cut to size and written on with ink. Birch bark is fragile and flakes when dry, so surviving examples are rare and precious.

Among the oldest Indian manuscripts are Gandharan Buddhist texts on birch bark in Kharosthi script, dated to around the 1st century CE and now held mostly in collections abroad. The Bakhshali manuscript, a mathematical text on birch bark found in 1881 near Peshawar and now in the Bodleian Library, Oxford, is famous for its use of a dot as a zero placeholder; radiocarbon dating published in 2017 gave a range of dates for different leaves, and its exact age is still discussed. In Kashmir, birch bark was widely used for Sanskrit manuscripts in [Sharada script](sarada-script.html).

Across most of India, and above all in the south and east, the standard material was palm leaf, from the talipot or palmyra palm. Leaves were dried, boiled or otherwise treated, smoothed and cut into long narrow strips. Two methods were used. In the south and Odisha, letters were incised with a metal stylus and the leaf was then rubbed with lamp black or charcoal mixed with oil so that the scratches showed dark. In the north and west, scribes wrote with a pen and ink on the leaf surface.

Holes were punched through the leaves, and a cord passed through them held the stack between two wooden covers, often painted. This long, narrow format (called pothi) shaped Indian book design even after paper arrived. Palm leaf survives better than birch bark but still needs care: insects, fungus and brittleness are constant threats.

Paper reached India from Central Asia and the Islamic world and became common in many regions from around the 13th and 14th centuries. Jain libraries in Gujarat and Rajasthan hold some of the earliest dated paper manuscripts in India, and Persian manuscripts of the Delhi Sultanate and Mughal courts were written on paper from the start. Over time paper largely replaced palm leaf in the north, while palm leaf remained in use in parts of the south and Odisha into the 19th and even 20th centuries.
Paper allowed illustrated manuscripts on a new scale, from Jain Kalpasutras to Mughal and Rajput painted books. Many kept the long pothi shape at first before bound volumes took over.

paras: The National Mission for Manuscripts (NMM) was set up in 2003 by the Government of India under the Ministry of Culture, working with the Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts in New Delhi. Its work covers surveying and documenting manuscripts in public and private hands, building a national database, preventive and curative conservation, digitisation, training in scripts and manuscriptology, and publication of unpublished texts. It works through partner centres across the country.

Check the NMM's own website for current programmes and access to its catalogue, since schemes and names change over time. Several state archives, the Oriental Research Institutes (such as those at Pune, Mysuru and Thiruvananthapuram) and university libraries also hold large catalogued collections.

Working with manuscripts needs three skills: the language, the script, and an understanding of the object. A Sanskrit text may be written in Sharada, Grantha, Bengali, Nandinagari or Devanagari, with scribal abbreviations and corrections in the margins. That is why script training matters as much as language study. The [Brahmi workshop](write-like-asoka-s-scribes-a-brahmi-workshop.html) and the scripts lecture give the background.

Preservation is the other half. Simple measures, such as stable humidity, protection from insects and light, and careful handling, prevent much loss. Talaash Heritage runs a [preventive conservation](caring-for-collections-preventive-conservation-basics.html) session that covers these basics for collections of all kinds, alongside the Sharada script course.

faq.q: What is the oldest manuscript found in India?
faq.a: There is no single agreed answer. The oldest surviving Indian manuscripts are birch bark Buddhist texts from Gandhara, around the 1st century CE. Within present-day India, some palm leaf and birch bark manuscripts from the late first millennium CE survive, and the Bakhshali manuscript's dating is still debated.

faq.q: How were palm leaf manuscripts made?
faq.a: Palm leaves were dried, treated, smoothed and cut into strips. Scribes either incised letters with a metal stylus and rubbed in lamp black, or wrote in ink. Holes were punched so that a cord could bind the leaves between wooden covers.

faq.q: What is the National Mission for Manuscripts?
faq.a: A Government of India initiative started in 2003 under the Ministry of Culture to locate, document, conserve and digitise India's manuscripts. It maintains a national database and works through partner centres for survey, conservation and training across the country.

faq.q: How many manuscripts are there in India?
faq.a: Estimates run into the millions, and many are still in private or temple collections that have not been catalogued. The NMM has documented several million, but numbers change as surveys continue, so treat any single figure as approximate.

faq.q: Why were Indian manuscripts long and narrow?
faq.a: The shape came from palm leaves, which are naturally long and narrow. The format, called pothi, was so standard that early paper manuscripts often copied it, with loose leaves stacked between covers rather than bound.

posts.hook: India's books were long and narrow because of palm leaves.
posts.caption: The pothi format came from the shape of the leaf. Even when paper arrived, scribes kept the same shape for centuries.

posts.hook: Got an old family manuscript? Don't laminate it.
posts.caption: Keep it dry, away from sunlight, wrapped in clean cotton cloth, and handle it with clean, dry hands. Then contact a manuscript library or conservator for advice.
